description: We're building Agrolog.IA for the Field Shift challenge. It compares crop rotations for Ecuador's Sierra across hundreds of simulated climate scenarios instead of average weather. The inputs will be NASA POWER, NEX-GDDP, IMERG and SMAP data, plus national yield records from INEC. We've confirmed we can access all of it. We're short on agronomy and crop modeling knowledge, remote sensing, and someone to build the web interface. If you've worked with Andean farmers, even better.
summary: Agrolog.IA shows farmers in Chimborazo and Carchi how each crop has performed from 2014 to 2025: typical yield, yield in a bad year, and how often losses happened. It combines INEC yield records with NASA POWER weather and checks whether losses matched dry seasons. We also built a water-balance model and tested it against three independent observations: INEC yields, MODIS NDVI, and SMAP root-zone soil moisture. The model passed none of the tests, and we report that openly. We therefore do not recommend crop rotations yet. The current output is a risk profile per crop, to bring to a local technician. Next steps are agronomist input and production-cost data.
details:
Agrolog.IA turns NASA and INEC data into a risk profile for each crop in two Ecuadorian provinces, Chimborazo and Carchi. For six crops (potato, barley, wheat, dry corn, faba bean, dry pea), the farmer report shows the typical yield from 2014 to 2025, the yield a farmer can expect in a bad year, and the years with losses above 30 %. It also checks whether those losses coincided with dry seasons. The answer is that they rarely did: in Chimborazo one of five loss years was dry, and in Carchi one of seven. Rain alone does not explain most losses, so pests, frost, and management also matter.

The farmer report is an explicit deliverable. It is a static web page generated from the public data by scripts/farmer_report.py. It shows, for each province, the crop tables (typical yield, bad-year yield, years with losses above 30 %) and the dry-season check. The page is not stored in the repository; running the script produces it.

We built a single-tank water-balance model to estimate crop water stress. We tested it against three independent observations, each with a rule written down before the data were analyzed: INEC yields for held-out years, MODIS NDVI, and SMAP root-zone soil moisture. The model did not pass any test. The NDVI test could not be evaluated at Chimborazo, because too few composites passed the quality and reference-year filters. The soil-moisture test showed a correlation no better than rainfall alone. We report these results in full, and we do not recommend crop rotations until the model is validated.

The intended impact is a clearer, more honest starting point for a farmer and a local technician. The project is creative in three ways: it uses NASA soil-moisture and vegetation data alongside official yield records; it tests the model against independent observations; and it reports the failures, which a farmer or a judge can check for themselves.

Tools: Python 3.14 (xarray, numpy, pyhdf, openpyxl, earthaccess, h5py), NASA AppEEARS for point extraction, and Claude (Anthropic) for code and text. Factors considered: data availability, provincial scale, the mismatch between satellite pixels and fields, and the difference between a model and a validated recommendation.
projectRefs: INEC ESPAC 2014–2025, crop yields and areas by province
